title: How do Steam fans think about playing - and switching - co-op games?
author: Simon Carless
excerpt: We did a survey. Also: the latest GameDiscoverCo Show & platform news.

How do Steam fans think about playing - and switching - co-op games?
We did a survey. Also: the latest GameDiscoverCo Show and platform news....
Simon Carless
Nov 25, 2026
[The GameDiscoverCo game discovery newsletter is written by ‘how people find your game’ expert & company founder Simon Carless, and is a regular look at how people discover and buy video games in the 2020s.]
This is your only GDCo newsletter this week (none on Fri, due to U.S. Thanksgiving!) First, two post-launch GTA nuggets: first, thx, PushSquare for a story on PSN not going down at launch . (Sony/Xbox did good!) And second, check the full GTA VI radio station soundtrack for the real reason we’re playing the game… (Mm, Star Chasers .)
Before we start, kudos to Devolver for counter-programming GTA’s launch day with Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed , their 2D faux-mascot platformer adventure. But look - somebody was urban exploring in Austin just before release and ‘found’ a Game Boy Advance demo version - Volvy’s Adventure: DX . (That’s a lotta trouble to go to…)
[ NEED THE BEST DATA? You can get a free demo of our GameDiscoverCo Pro company-wide ‘Steam deep dive’ & console data, inc. MCP server, by reaching out today - >110 orgs have it. Or, signing up to GDCo Basic gets extra newsletter and Discord access, plus more .]
Game discovery news: no drunken asteroid dirt..
Starting (and ending?) the week in style, here’s what news we see from a game discovery & platform point of view:
The latest ‘trending wishlists’ for unreleased Steam games , per GDCo Pro, we saw incremental mining game No Asteroids (#1) & physics-based heavy machinery sim Dirt Town (#3) make the Top 3, alongside the better-known Drunken Goddess Reflux (#2), a ‘drinking shots vs. a demon’ anime Russian roulette roguelite.
New at #4, Mondrayn is a "grim JRPG with survival elements" - lots of dark/creepy pixel art here. On the other hand, Winx Club - Moonlight Quest (#5) brings back the popular European '00s animated series as a bright open-world actioner. (Also charting: Ebbtide, Family Time, Deadlock, Dear Passengers, you know the drill.)
Engines as platforms: Unreal Engine 6 will not launch with the engine's long-standard Blueprints scripting system , according to Epic, with VP Marcus Wassmer saying: “with recent advances in AI capability, we expect AI to massively help with converting UE5 projects to UE6.” (Blueprints will still work in UE5, though.)
ICYMI: Grand Theft Auto VI sold 32.5m pre-release and had (estimated) day one retail sales of $3.79 billion , according to Rockstar. (It’s now officially 39m unique players on PlayStation alone , and GDCo estimates ~75% PlayStation and ~25% Xbox - so that’s ~50m total, rite?) Also: Circana notes a >2.4x PS and >2.3x Xbox YoY U.S. hardware sales increase , w/e Nov. 7th - a few days before release, even.
Two interesting Steam Machine stock updates from Valve: first, the 512GB model ($1,049 without controller) is now 100% in-stock and buyable now. Secondly, they are “closing the waitlist to additional signups” for the 2TB model, partly due to “supply constraints for hardware components.” There’ll be more info on January, but they say “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels.”
Meta news: director of games Chris Pruett recently wrote a ‘state of Meta VR x games’ post, noting Jan-Sept 2026 $ “steady compared with the same period last year, even without a new device launch”, with “hundreds of millions of dollars” in dev $. One weirder stat: “For the developers in the Meta Horizon+ [Game Pass-like] program, 80% now earn more from MH+ than from the store.”
Xbox is further digging out from its tech debt for ‘Xbox on PC’ clients, as Windows Central notes: “One long-standing complaint about PC games on the Microsoft Store is the lack of support for mods” , but a recent update to the Xbox app on PC has Into The Breach as an example game with an ‘enable mods’ tickbox.
In ‘more clone wars’ news, Patrick Klepek wrote something about ‘ art copying’ game Sloppy Forgeries and various ‘fast follows’ of its high hook idea , citing me as saying a) there’s not much new under the sun b) Roblox clones don’t matter much to Steam players. (The devs did DMCA another Steam game based on ‘look & feel’ , but - plot twist - Sloppy Forgeries itself topped out at just 55 CCU.)
GameStop is now largely a Pokemon card pack-scalper, but CEO Ryan Cohen grokked that ‘no more physical games’ is a problem for ‘em, saying to Bloomberg : “When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it, or lend it to a friend… the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it’s also hurt GameStop.”
Steam has shipped an extensive UI & feature refresh for its Community Market feature , whch allows players to P2P buy and sell in-game items - by $, it’s largely used for Valve titles like Counter-Strike 2 & DOTA, but games like Don’t Starve Together & Rust also use it. (Here’s the full list of compatible games .)
Microlinks: very unofficial remote play app Asobi had its direct PS5 cloud streaming blocked , tho remote play still works; the finalists for the 2026 Apple App Store awards inc. Ball x Pit, Big Walk, Crimson Desert; more decompilation of mobile games says Monopoly Go! gives everyone the same 80 dice rolls to start.
OUR SPONSOR: creators.gg , Where Streamers Find Your Game
Creator outreach is miserable. You know it, we know it, your inbox knows it. creators.gg is the thing we built so you can stop doing the worst bits. Build a campaign on FirstLook, post it, streamers apply, you approve the creators you want repping your game.
Small streamers to seasoned partners, all on one platform. Oh, and we just plugged it straight into the Twitch Dashboard , so eligible streamers find your game where they already stream. Pretty handy!
Eden (our CEO) will demo it himself . GDCo subscribers: 30-day free Pro trial, worth $1,599.
How Steam fans think & act re: co-op games…
There’s no doubt that the rise of co-op games as an actual discovery method - ‘my friends are playing this game together, I should hop on too!’ - is one of the big trends in PC games over the past few years. One key reason: co-op more easily and virally traverses the extreme ‘filter bubble’ many players are in, vs. single-player games.
But we at GameDiscoverCo are continually frustrated that nobody asks a mass of players whether - and how - they play co-op games. So in our quarterly survey of our Steam Fan Snapshot survey audience , we asked a subset of them - just over 5,500 - about their co-op game habits. And here’s what they said:
Firstly - and remember, we’re asking ‘Steam fans’ who are active buyers & pay attention online to giveaways, etc - only 24% of this audience said they mainly play single player games . That leaves >75% who are multiplayer-compatible. Of those:
29.3% say they play online co-op games across multiple sessions every week.
21.4% do play co-op, but less often: ‘once every one or two weeks’.
17.9% play much more seldom: ‘a few times per year’.
7.4% are ‘mainly PvP multiplayer’ focused (not actually a huge percentage!)
Nothing very surprising in here - although it does show how prevalent online co-op play (with voice chat) is, something that can feel like a surprise if you’re a little older and your friends don’t do it. In many ways, co-op games are a ‘ third place ’ for a lot of people.
We also asked about the cohort co-op gamers actually play with, and the results are also diverse:
According to the survey, 37% of those who play co-op do it with “the exact same friend crew” all of the time - that’s the highest result by far. Of the other answers:
25.9% of the respondents have a “similar core crew, with some people rotating.”
17.5% switch between multiple friend groups, each playing their own set of games.
19.6% - a minority, but still important - play with “mainly people met through matchmaking.”
For me, this gives a much better mental model than I had about how core Steam gamers (from a worldwide sample) might approach co-op. (It’s a very large cohort, and they’re mainly people who know each other.)
But we did ask one more question, a ‘literal’ one where respondents could type what they wanted, around ‘How often do you switch the online co-op game you are playing?’ We queried whether friendslop made rotation faster, since the games are cheaper. We got ~2,000 (!) usable responses. Here’s some trends we spotted from those replies:
Cheaper games do lower the overall cost to get an entire friend group in: one respondent said: “The cheaper pricing (like below $10 or $5) helps with more people in the group picking games up” , and discount sales for expensive games can matter because “many friends wouldn’t buy [a specific game] at full price.”
There’s evidence that ‘reluctant buyers’ will come along with a friend group: one player says: “I can play the [current] game more, but they wanna play something else and I go [along] with them”, and “getting dragged into random games with friends” was another response. If the majority want to play, everyone in the group is buying!
While price is important, lack of time is still the key factor : we got some gentle pushback on $ being the only arbiter, including: “The price wasn't the barrier, it's our schedules lol.” , and “We can't fit many sessions into our busy schedules.” This is especially true as players get older and become “working professionals.”
There’s evidence that players don’t constantly churn co-op games. One said: “We've been revisiting the same 3-4 games over the past year, with a ~65/15/10/10 split.” And another explains a three-way fork: “MMOs and live service competitive games stay long term, some repeating ‘old slop’ games… medium term, and trending stuff for a month/week.”
So it does seem like there’s well-designed smaller co-op games - like Peak and R.E.P.O. (above), both cited multiple times in the survey - that keep people’s interest & partially block new entrants. And there’s bigger PvE titles like Helldivers 2, too. (Multiple players cited Battle Pass-likes and timed rewards in bigger-budget games.)
And of course, there’s big PvP or PvPvE games in the mix - which are truly ‘live service’- d, provide a lot of retention, and constantly roll out neat updates. One person said it’s “hard to convince my friends to spend money on a new game… when Fortnite is right there with bi-weekly updates.”
So - it’s complex, and there’s a lot of choice. But think of it like this: co-op isn’t just a mode to add to your game , it’s the magic ability to add you to the menu of possible games that millions of friend groups discuss playing together ! It’s not easy to become ‘dish of the day’, of course. But you should at least know how it all works….
GameDiscoverCo Show: the mega-trends of 2026
The first of two end-of-year GameDiscover Show specials is here, ft. myself (Simon) and Post Games’ Chris Plante ruminating on the big issues. Reminder: sub to the podcast via Apple Podcasts , Spotify & elsewhere (audio), with a video version on YouTube (above).
It's been quite a year in video game discovery & platforms. So in the first of a two-part EOY extravaganza (with the second coming during the Xmas holidays!), Simon and Chris look at a bunch of the megatrends in the PC/console game biz this year, from RAM shortages & friendslop to AA woes and Xbox's direction of travel.

title: Game Oracle v7.4: Small Steps Forward
author: Ross Burton, PhD
text:
Game Oracle v7.4: Small Steps Forward
Share:
Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Devlogs
Published: 11/25/2026
Updated: 11/25/2026
If you've been following Game Oracle's progress, you'll have noticed that our release cadence has stepped up a notch recently. Releases within version 7 are going to be smaller and more frequent. There are three reasons for this:
I've grown tired of bundling everything into big releases. It doesn't help my stress levels, and it means you don't get to enjoy improvements to the platform until I've sorted my life out!
We're working on this full-time now. I feel like I've finally got my testing and release pipeline into a good state, so shipping often no longer means shipping nervously.
We're making our own game, Pixel Pyros, with Game Oracle. Using the platform every day brings lots of little issues to light, so our own game dev experience gets to drive Game Oracle forward.
So today we're bringing you v7.4.0, a small update that makes collecting market data and designing your game a little smoother. Expect many more releases like this going forward.
Folders in your Scrapbook
The Scrapbook is where everything you clip while researching ends up. After a few weeks of working on Pixel Pyros, some of our sections had grown long enough that finding one particular capsule or review quote meant a lot of scrolling.
Every Scrapbook section can now hold folders. Open a section such as Images or Snippets, choose New folder , give it a name, and start filing it up. You can drag a clipping onto a folder, or use the Move to folder  option in its menu if you'd rather not drag. New clips still land loose in their section, so clipping stays as quick as it was, and you can tidy up whenever it suits you.
Folders belong to the project, so everyone on your team sees the same ones. Renaming a folder is done in place. Deleting one never deletes your clippings, which simply go back to the section they came from.
Your recent work, one click away
Most days we bounce between the same handful of files, like the game design document, a whiteboard of art ideas, and the marketing workboard. Getting back to them used to mean going through Project Home every time.
There's now a star just left of Dashboard in the navbar. Click it to see the three things you opened most recently, followed by your favourites. Both lists work across projects, so if you're juggling more than one game, you can jump straight into the right file. To add a favourite, star an item from its editor toolbar, from its tile menu on Project Home, or from the Project Items list. Your shortcuts are personal to you and follow you between devices. On mobile, you'll find the same lists in the menu under Recent and favourites .
Copy where a file lives
Every item page now has a small copy button at the end of its breadcrumb. Click it and you'll get the file's full path as plain text, like Pixel Pyros / Art / Fireworks . We added it because we kept typing these paths by hand, whether we were linking related work in a document or telling an AI assistant which file to look at.
Better tables in documents
Our game design document has some long tables in it, so tables got the most attention in this release.
The table toolbar stays with you. In a long table, the toolbar now pins just below the navbar as you scroll, so adding a row halfway down no longer means scrolling back to the top.
Rows can move. Click a row and choose Move up or Move down , or press Alt+Shift+↑ or ↓. The header row always stays at the top.
Columns can be resized. Drag the right edge of any column to make it wider or narrower. If you'd rather use buttons or the keyboard, Narrower and Wider in the toolbar do the same thing, and Even widths puts everything back to equal. Column widths are saved with your document. Markdown tables have no way to store widths, so they aren't included when you export to Markdown.
What's next
None of these changes are big on their own, but they're exactly the kind of friction we hit while working on Pixel Pyros, and we suspect you've hit some of them too. If something in Game Oracle slows you down, let us know. It's the fastest way to get it into one of these smaller releases.

Copy where a file lives

Every item page now has a small copy button at the end of its breadcrumb. Click it and you'll get the file's full path as plain text, like Pixel Pyros / Art / Fireworks. We added it because we kept typing these paths by hand, whether we were linking related work in a document or telling an AI assistant which file to look at.

Better tables in documents

Our game design document has some long tables in it, so tables got the most attention in this release.

  • The table toolbar stays with you. In a long table, the toolbar now pins just below the navbar as you scroll, so adding a row halfway down no longer means scrolling back to the top.
  • Rows can move. Click a row and choose Move up or Move down, or press Alt+Shift+↑ or ↓. The header row always stays at the top.
  • Columns can be resized. Drag the right edge of any column to make it wider or narrower. If you'd rather use buttons or the keyboard, Narrower and Wider in the toolbar do the same thing, and Even widths puts everything back to equal. Column widths are saved with your document. Markdown tables have no way to store widths, so they aren't included when you export to Markdown.

What's next

None of these changes are big on their own, but they're exactly the kind of friction we hit while working on Pixel Pyros, and we suspect you've hit some of them too. If something in Game Oracle slows you down, let us know. It's the fastest way to get it into one of these smaller releases.
